Links: [{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/ocrmypdf-appleocr/0.4.1/"},{"title":"Plugin to run OCRmyPDF with Apple Vision Framework OCR engine","url":"https://pypi.org/project/ocrmypdf-appleocr/"},{"title":"OCRmyPDF AppleOCR","url":"https://github.com/mkyt/OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR"},{"title":"ocrmypdf appleocr","url":"https://socket.dev/pypi/package/ocrmypdf-appleocr"},{"title":"socket.dev","url":"https://socket.dev/pypi/package/ocrmypdf-appleocr/overview/0.3.1"},{"title":"trendshift.io","url":"https://trendshift.io/repositories/306562"},{"title":"OCRmyPDF AppleOCR","url":"https://hn.jakechampion.name/reader/https://github.com/mkyt/OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR"}]

The OCRmyPDF AppleOCR plugin is a macOS-only add-on that lets OCRmyPDF use Apple's Vision framework for text recognition. The latest version I found is 0.4.1, and it requires OCRmyPDF 17 or later.

- **Recognition modes:** The plugin offers fast, accurate, and livetext modes. The default is livetext on macOS 13 and later, and accurate on macOS 12 and earlier.
- **Underlying APIs:** The fast and accurate modes use VNRecognizeTextRequest from Apple's Vision framework. Livetext uses VisionKit's ImageAnalyzer, which is officially Swift-only, but can be accessed via private API (VKCImageAnalyzer) through pyobjc. That private-API dependency is a fragility worth knowing about.
- **Installation and use:** The plugin registers itself as an OCRmyPDF entry point, so it is loaded automatically once installed. Older OCRmyPDF versions need the explicit `--plugin ocrmypdf_appleocr` flag instead.
- **Renderer:** sandwich is the recommended renderer and the plugin's default, because OCRmyPDF's built-in fpdf2 renderer currently places the invisible text layer incorrectly for both rotated and some pages.
- **Limitations:** Automatic language detection (und) is not supported in livetext mode.
- **Language support:** The 0.4.1 page lists English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish for macOS Tahoe 26. The older 0.3.1 listing on Socket shows a much longer list including Japanese and Chinese, so the two sources disagree on coverage, likely because of version differences. I'd check the current README before relying on either list.

Web search results for query: "PDFMathTranslate-next pdf2zh_next BabelDOC ollama scanned PDF OCR workaround"

Links: [{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/babeldoc-stream/0.6.4.post3/"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/babeldoc/0.6.4/"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/funstory-ai/BabelDOC"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/BeringLab/BabelDOC"},{"title":"Yet Another Document Translator","url":"https://pypi.org/p/BabelDOC"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/BabelDOC/"},{"title":"pdf2zh next","url":"https://pdf2zh-next.com"}]

The search turned up BabelDOC's OCR workaround options, but nothing specific to running pdf2zh_next with Ollama on scanned PDFs.

- **What the workaround does:** White rectangular blocks are added below the translation to cover the original text, and all text is forced to black. The docs say it is only suitable for documents with black text on white background.
- **Flag details:** One README describes it as a way to fill background for scanned PDF, with the assumption that the background is pure white and the text is pure black. It also says this option will also auto enable --skip-scanned-detection.
- **Automatic variant:** A separate --auto-enable-ocr-workaround flag will attempt to enable OCR processing and skip further scan detection if a document is detected as heavily scanned.
- **Ollama:** BabelDOC's docs say for local models like Ollama, you can use any value as the API key, which implies connecting through its OpenAI-compatible option. Only OpenAI-compatible LLM is supported, so for more translator support, use PDFMathTranslate.
- **Project context:** PDFMathTranslate-next is the project that adds BabelDOC support for self-deployment plus a WebUI with more translation services.

Caveats: I didn't find pdf2zh_next-specific instructions for the OCR workaround, and the sources are mostly BabelDOC CLI docs, so the exact flag names may differ in the pdf2zh_next frontend. The workaround also only suits scans with black text on a white background. I'd suggest checking the PDFMathTranslate-next repo for its current option names and the Ollama setup.

Web search results for query: "MinerU Apple Silicon mlx vlm backend install 2026"

Links: [{"title":"mlx vlm","url":"https://anaconda.org/cf-post-staging/mlx-vlm"},{"title":"github.com%2Fopendatalab%2Fmineru vl utils","url":"https://awesome.ecosyste.ms/projects/github.com%2Fopendatalab%2Fmineru-vl-utils"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/mcp-mineru/0.1.2/"},{"title":"github opendatalab/MinerU mineru-2.6.3-released","url":"https://newreleases.io/project/github/opendatalab/MinerU/release/mineru-2.6.3-released"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/mineru-vl-utils/0.2.5/"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/mineru-vl-utils/0.1.15/"},{"title":"pypi.org","url":"https://pypi.org/project/mineru-vl-utils/0.2.6/"}]

I found no 2026-specific install guide, but the results cover the current setup for MinerU's MLX backend on Apple Silicon.

- **Backend availability:** MinerU 2.6.3 added a `vlm-mlx-engine` backend for MinerU2.5 on Apple Silicon. Compared to the vlm-transformers backend, vlm-mlx-engine delivers a 100%–200% speed improvement. The changelog lists macOS 13.5 as the minimum for MLX, with 14.0 or later recommended MLX requires macOS 13.5 or later, recommended for use with version 14.0 or higher.. The same page says the latest releases are in the 3.0.x series, so the 2.6.3 notes may be dated.
- **Python package route:** For the `mineru-vl-utils` package, the mlx-engine backend needs the MLX extra. The PyPI page gives pip install -U "mineru-vl-utils[mlx]". Its example loads the model with `mlx_vlm`'s loader using the MinerU2.5-2509-1.2B checkpoint, then passes the model and processor to `MinerUClient` with `backend="mlx-engine"`.
- **Third-party MCP wrapper:** An unofficial package, mcp-mineru, exposes a `vlm-mlx-engine` option. Its listed install is a single `uvx` command for Claude Code. On an M4 with 16GB, the author reports about 38s per page for vlm-mlx-engine, versus about 148s per page for vlm-transformers and about 32s per page for the CPU-only pipeline backend.

The results don't confirm exact 2026 install steps or the current versions of `mlx-vlm` and `mineru-vl-utils`. Check the MinerU GitHub README and the PyPI pages for the latest commands.

content.text:
I've assumed you have an Apple Silicon Mac with 16 GB of RAM or more, that the documents are in a European language printed in Roman type (for example German or French), and that you're translating into English. I haven't run anything on your machine. I checked the current state of these tools on the web, but I haven't tested them on your scans.

## Main recommendation: Apple's own OCR, then layout-preserving translation with a local LLM

**The OCR Safari uses already runs locally on your Mac.** Safari's "translate text in image" uses Apple's Vision/Live Text engine, which runs on the Mac itself. The plugin **OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR** lets you run that same engine on a whole batch. That should close most of the gap you saw with Tesseract.

The pipeline:

1. **OCRmyPDF + AppleOCR plugin** turns each scan into a searchable PDF. The text is placed exactly where it appears on the page.
2. **pdf2zh-next (PDFMathTranslate-next, built on BabelDOC)** reads that text layer and its layout. It translates each block with a **local LLM through Ollama** and writes a translated PDF with the text in the original positions. It can also write a side-by-side bilingual PDF, which is very useful for research.

Nothing leaves your machine.

### Install

```bash
# Prerequisites (Homebrew)
brew install pipx uv ollama ghostscript tesseract
pipx ensurepath

# 1) OCR: OCRmyPDF + Apple Vision plugin (the plugin needs OCRmyPDF ≥ 17, same environment)
pipx install ocrmypdf
pipx inject ocrmypdf ocrmypdf-appleocr

# 2) Local LLM
ollama serve &               # or start the Ollama app
ollama pull qwen3:14b        # good multilingual model for 16–32 GB; use qwen3:8b on 16 GB if it's slow,
                             # or a larger/newer model if you have the RAM

# 3) Layout-preserving translator
uv tool install --python 3.12 pdf2zh-next
```

### First run (try 10 varied pages first, not all 1,000)

```bash
# Combine page images into a PDF (img2pdf comes with OCRmyPDF)
img2pdf scans/batch01/*.jpg -o batch01.pdf

# OCR with Apple Vision (plugin loads automatically; check `ocrmypdf --help` for its options
# such as recognition mode and language)
ocrmypdf --rotate-pages --deskew -l deu batch01.pdf batch01_ocr.pdf

# Translate: easiest first time via the web UI
pdf2zh_next --gui
```

In the web UI:
- Choose **Ollama** (or "OpenAI-compatible" with base URL `http://localhost:11434/v1` and any API key) as the service.
- Pick your model, then set the source and target languages.
- For scans, turn on the **OCR workaround**. It covers the original text with white boxes and draws the translation on top. It assumes black text on a white background, so very yellowed pages may look patchy.

Once the settings work, switch to the CLI for batches (`pdf2zh_next --help`; flag names change between versions). Leave it running overnight.

## Alternatives, depending on what fails

- **The layout is complex and the reading order comes out scrambled** (columns, sidebars, tables, footnotes): use **MinerU**. It has a fast `vlm-mlx-engine` backend for Apple Silicon. It produces Markdown/JSON in the correct reading order, which you then translate with the same Ollama model. You lose the exact visual layout but keep the structure. One user reported about 38 s per page on an M4 with 16 GB, so 1,000 pages would take about 10 hours. Install: `uv tool install "mineru[all]"`, then see its README for the MLX backend. For research, a "scan on the left, structured translation on the right" view is often more useful than a pixel-perfect re-render.
- **The print is badly degraded and OCR garbles it:** use a vision-language model, for example Qwen-VL via Ollama or LM Studio. Prompt it per page with "transcribe, then translate, keep headings/columns as Markdown". These models read damaged print much better than classic OCR, but they sometimes invent plausible text. Keep the transcription alongside the translation so you can check it.
- **The documents are in blackletter (Fraktur)**: Apple Vision handles it poorly. Use Tesseract's dedicated models (`-l deu_latf`) or Kraken/Calamari with a historical-print model in step 1, and keep step 2 the same.

## Practical notes

- **Skip phkhanhtrinh23/translation_layoutrecovery.** It's an older research prototype with pinned dependencies. pdf2zh-next/BabelDOC does the same job and is actively maintained.
- **Clean the scans before OCR.** Deskewing, cropping borders and scanning at 300 dpi or more help OCR more than switching engines does.
- **Keep the translation model consistent.** Use one model and a short glossary of recurring names and terms for the whole collection, so terminology stays the same across pages.

Sources:
- [OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR (GitHub)](https://github.com/mkyt/OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/ocrmypdf-appleocr/)
- [BabelDOC (GitHub)](https://github.com/funstory-ai/BabelDOC) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/BabelDOC/) · [pdf2zh-next](https://pdf2zh-next.com)
- [MinerU MLX backend release notes](https://newreleases.io/project/github/opendatalab/MinerU/release/mineru-2.6.3-released) · [mineru-vl-utils](https://pypi.org/project/mineru-vl-utils/0.2.6/) · [mcp-mineru (speed figures)](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-mineru/0.1.2/)
